title: IFCLoRA: Topology-Aware Rank Allocation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a widely used parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for large language models, but its performance depends strongly on how a fixed rank budget is distributed across Transformer modules. Existing adaptive-rank methods usually rely on local gradient statistics collected during training, which introduces extra memory and computation and overlooks task-conditioned global information flow. We propose IFCLoRA, a topology-aware rank allocation method applied before fine-tuning. Using a small calibration set and a frozen pretrained model, IFCLoRA builds a sparse task-conditioned interaction graph whose nodes represent LoRA-compatible modules. It combines a global information-flow topology prior with local gradient sensitivity to compute Information-Flow Centrality scores, which estimate each module's adaptation importance under multi-hop propagation. Ranks are then assigned once under a global budget. Across multiple models, tasks, and low-rank settings, IFCLoRA consistently outperforms LoRA, AdaLoRA, and EVA under matched training configurations and total rank budgets, while retaining training costs comparable to standard LoRA. On mathematical reasoning with LLaMA 3 8B, IFCLoRA improves over LoRA by 1.36 percent at rank 4 and 1.82 percent at rank 8. Further analysis shows task-dependent, non-uniform rank profiles, indicating that global information-flow structure provides an informative and interpretable prior for low-budget parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

B Additional Results C Analysis C.1 Hyperparameter Sensitivity C.2 Calibration Size Sensitivity C.3 Rank Distribution Visualization D Budget and Efficiency Analysis D.1 Trainable Parameter Counts D.2 Runtime and Memory Overhead License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2607.22251v1 [cs.LG] 24 Jul 2026 IFCLoRA: Topology-Aware Rank Allocation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning Wei Zhang Faculty of Artificial Intelligence in Education Laboratory for Artificial Intelligence and New Forms of Education Central China Normal University Wuhan, Hubei, China &Xinwu Liu Faculty of Artificial Intelligence in Education Laboratory for Artificial Intelligence and New Forms of Education Central China Normal University Wuhan, Hubei, China &Yihang Cheng Faculty of Artificial Intelligence in Education Laboratory for Artificial Intelligence and New Forms of Education Central China Normal University Wuhan, Hubei, China Corresponding author: yihangcheng@mails.ccnu.edu.cn Abstract Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a prominent parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for large language models, yet its effectiveness is critically shaped by how a fixed rank budget is allocated across Transformer modules. Existing adaptive-rank LoRA variants typically reallocate ranks using training-time local gradient statistics, incurring additional memory and computational overhead. However, this local sensitivity-driven view leaves the role of task-conditioned global information-flow structure in rank allocation largely underexplored. To address this gap, we propose IFCLoRA (Information-Flow Centrality LoRA), a topology-aware, pre-fine-tuning rank allocation procedure. IFCLoRA performs lightweight tracing on a frozen pretrained model using a small calibration set, constructing a task-conditioned sparse interaction graph whose nodes correspond to LoRA-insertable modules. The method then combines a global information-flow topology prior with node-wise local gradient sensitivity to compute Information-Flow Centrality (IFC) scores, which quantify each node’s adaptation importance under task-conditioned multi-hop propagation. Finally, IFCLoRA assigns discrete ranks in a single shot under a global rank constraint. Across models and tasks, under the same training setup and total rank budgets as representative baselines such as LoRA, AdaLoRA, and EVA, IFCLoRA consistently improves aggregate performance in multiple low-rank regimes while incurring training-time costs comparable to standard LoRA. For example, when fine-tuning LLaMA3-8B for mathematical reasoning, IFCLoRA improves over LoRA by 1.36% and 1.82% at rank 4 and rank 8, respectively. Further analyses reveal task-dependent, non-uniform allocation patterns in the learned rank profiles, providing an interpretable view of how adaptation capacity is distributed and suggesting that task-conditioned global information-flow topology can serve as an informative structural prior for low-budget PEFT. 1 Introduction Large pretrained language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong generalization ability across a wide range of natural language processing and reasoning tasks (Vaswani et al. , 2017 ; Grattafiori et al. , 2024 ; Yang et al. , 2025 ) . However, as model sizes continue to grow, full fine-tuning faces prohibitively high memory and storage costs. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has accordingly emerged as a practical paradigm for adapting large models with limited trainable parameters (Han et al. , 2024 ) . Among PEFT methods, LoRA parameterizes weight updates as low-rank matrix products, substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters while maintaining competitive performance (Hu et al. , 2022 ) . Standard LoRA assigns the same rank to all target layers and modules, implicitly assuming that different positions contribute similarly to the task. In low-budget settings, however, Transformer layers and modules exhibit substantial functional heterogeneity. Prior analyses of Transformer circuits and feed-forward memories further suggest that attention heads, FFN blocks, and residual pathways play distinct roles in information processing (Geva et al. , 2021 ; Wang et al. , 2022 ; Meng et al. , 2022 ; Syed et al. , 2024 ) . These components differ in how they store, route, and transform information. In low-budget regimes, model performance can be sensitive to whether limited capacity is concentrated on task-relevant information-propagation paths or spread uniformly. Although adaptive rank-allocation methods improve over uniform allocation (Zhang et al. , 2023 ; He et al. , 2025 ; Ed-dib et al. , 2025 ) , they still mainly rely on local statistics during training and introduce additional overhead. A natural question is therefore whether a global perspective that explicitly characterizes cross-layer information flow can provide a better allocation signal. Mechanistic interpretability reveals traceable task-relevant computational subgraphs (Conmy et al. , 2023 ; Syed et al. , 2024 ) . Graph centrality analysis provides tools for quantifying global node importance (Page et al. , 1999 ; Newman, 2018 ) . Yet these two perspectives have not been directly combined into a pre-fine-tuning rank-allocation mechanism. Figure 1 : Comparison of LoRA, AdaLoRA, and IFCLoRA rank-allocation strategies. Figure 1 compares standard LoRA, AdaLoRA, and IFCLoRA from the perspective of when and how ranks are allocated. To this end, we propose IFCLoRA, a topology-aware low-rank adaptation framework that completes rank allocation in a single pre-fine-tuning pass. Given a small calibration set, IFCLoRA performs lightweight tracing on a frozen model to construct a task-conditioned interaction graph, then fuses a topology prior with local gradient sensitivity into an Information-Flow Centrality score for one-shot budget-constrained rank routing. Experiments on GSM8K and SuperGLUE show that, under the same rank budget, IFCLoRA provides consistent GSM8K gains across three backbone models and a generally favorable but task-dependent SuperGLUE profile. Further analysis shows that the learned rank distribution varies across tasks and concentrates capacity on a small number of structurally important modules, providing a topology-based implementation of parameter routing in PEFT. The main contributions of this paper are: 1. We propose IFCLoRA, a topology-aware one-shot rank allocation method. IFCLoRA introduces task-conditioned interaction-graph construction and information-flow centrality analysis into PEFT, and completes discrete rank allocation under a global budget before fine-tuning begins. 2. We introduce the Information-Flow Centrality score, a heuristic importance measure that combines bidirectional graph reachability with local gradient sensitivity to produce a computable rank-allocation signal. 3. We validate IFCLoRA across multiple models, tasks, and budgets. Experiments on three backbone models cover mathematical reasoning and semantic understanding under low-rank budgets r = 4 r=4 and r = 8 r=8 . On GSM8K, IFCLoRA improves over LoRA by 1.13 percentage points on average and reaches a maximum single GSM8K gain of 1.82 percentage points. The learned rank distributions are task-specific and non-uniform. 2 Related Work 2.1 PEFT and Adaptive Rank Allocation Representative PEFT methods include Adapter Tuning (Houlsby et al. , 2019 ) , Prefix Tuning (Li and Liang, 2021 ) , Prompt Tuning (Lester et al. , 2021 ) , BitFit (Ben Zaken et al. , 2022 ) , IA3 (Liu et al. , 2022 ) , and LoRA (Hu et al. , 2022 ) . LoRA parameterizes the weight increment as a low-rank decomposition, 𝐖 = 𝐖 ( 0 ) + 𝐁𝐀 \mathbf{W}=\mathbf{W}^{(0)}+\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A} , where 𝐁 ∈ ℝ d 1 × r \mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times r} and 𝐀 ∈ ℝ r × d 2 \mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{2}} with r ≪ { d 1 , d 2 } r\ll\{d_{1},d_{2}\} . It greatly reduces trainable parameters and memory overhead, making it one of the most widely used PEFT baselines. The uniform rank allocation adopted by standard LoRA fails to account for the pervasive functional heterogeneity across layers and modules in Transformers. Recent work has therefore explored adaptive rank allocation from several directions: AdaLoRA and ALoRA estimate rank importance during optimization or under a fixed adaptation budget and redistribute capacity accordingly, EVA and TLoRA use downstream activations, variance, task-aware pre-fine-tuning signals, or sensitivity cues, GeLoRA and GoRA use representation geometry or gradient information, and IGU-LoRA and L1RA use attribution, uncertainty, or dynamic rank-assignment mechanisms (Zhang et al. , 2023 ; Liu et al. , 2024 ; Paischer et al. , 2025 ; Lin et al. , 2026 ; Ed-dib et al. , 2025 ; He et al. , 2025 ; Cui et al. , 2026 ; Sundararajan et al. , 2017 ; Singh et al. , 2025 ; Deng et al. , 2026 ) . These methods are closely related to IFCLoRA in their goal of avoiding uniform rank allocation, but their allocation signals are still primarily derived from local matrix-level, activation-level, gradient-level, attribution-level, geometric, dynamic-assignment, or training-time statistics. In contrast, IFCLoRA explicitly constructs a task-conditioned interaction graph and converts global source-to-sink information-flow topology into a pre-fine-tuning, one-shot rank-allocation prior, lightly calibrated by local gradient sensitivity. 2.2 Mechanistic Interpretability and Circuit Analysis Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand how neural networks realize specific functions by examining internal computational structure. Prior work suggests that language models contain traceable task-relevant computational subgraphs: attention heads, MLP layers, and residual pathways can jointly form circuits that implement specific functions (Elhage et al. , 2021 ; Wang et al. , 2022 ; Conmy et al. , 2023 ; Syed et al. , 2024 ; Hadad et al. , 2026 ) , while causal tracing and model editing locate localized computations that mediate factual recall (Meng et al. , 2022 ) . Studies of component roles further reveal the memory-like function of feed-forward networks (Geva et al. , 2021 ) . Although these methods reveal important structural regularities, they mostly belong to the post hoc analysis paradigm. The resulting graph structures have not yet been systematically used to guide parameter allocation before fine-tuning, and full circuit extraction is often computationally expensive. IFCLoRA borrows the idea of modeling internal interactions as a directed graph, but redirects it from post hoc explanation to pre-fine-tuning rank allocation. 2.3 Graph Centrality in Neural Networks Graph centrality is a classical tool in complex network analysis for measuring the relative importance of nodes in a global topology (Page et al. , 1999 ; Newman, 2018 ) . Deep neural networks have increasingly been abstracted as graph structures for architecture analysis and compression. Centrality scores such as PageRank, Katz centrality, betweenness centrality, and eigenvector centrality motivate global views of information flow for identifying important or redundant nodes (Yu et al. , 2026 ) . However, existing graph-centrality methods mainly serve static architecture analysis or offline model compression. For LLM adaptation, what affects downstream reasoning is not only whether a node is a static hub, but also whether it lies on a task-relevant path and acts as a mediator in multi-hop information propagation. To transfer graph centrality into PEFT, task-relevant local sensitivity must be integrated into the centrality measure. The IFC metric proposed here is designed for this purpose. Taken together, prior work shows that ranks should not be allocated uniformly and that downstream data, gradients, and attribution signals can provide useful allocation cues. IFCLoRA complements this line of work by introducing a task-conditioned topology prior: it estimates which nodes lie on source-to-sink information-flow paths and uses this prior for one-shot budget-constrained rank allocation before fine-tuning. The resulting gap is not task awareness per se, but the explicit conversion of global multi-hop information-flow topology into a rank-allocation prior for low-budget PEFT. 3 Method We propose IFCLoRA, a topology-aware rank allocation method for low-budget PEFT. Unlike LoRA and training-time dynamic methods such as AdaLoRA (Hu et al. , 2022 ; Zhang et al. , 2023 ) , IFCLoRA performs lightweight circuit tracing with a small calibration set before fine-tuning begins, constructs a task-conditioned interaction graph, and completes rank allocation in one shot. The method consists of four stages: task-conditioned interaction graph construction, topology-prior extraction, local sensitivity calibration, and budget-constrained rank allocation. Figure 2 : Overall framework of IFCLoRA. Given a small calibration set, IFCLoRA first performs lightweight tracing on a frozen Transformer and compares clean forward activations with target-unit activations after source-unit zero ablation to construct a task-conditioned interaction graph (a). It then extracts Information-Flow Centrality (IFC) from the graph based on forward and backward reachability from input-side and output-side anchors as a topology prior (b). Next, IFC is fused with type-wise normalized local task sensitivity to obtain module-level importance scores (c). Finally, under a total rank-budget constraint, one-shot rank routing allocates differentiated ranks to different layers and LoRA-insertable modules (d). Figure 2 illustrates the complete IFCLoRA workflow from calibration-based tracing to budget-constrained rank routing. 3.1 Problem Definition Let the pretrained Transformer be ℳ \mathcal{M} , and let 𝒰 = { u 1 , … , u U } \mathcal{U}=\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{U}\} denote all LoRA-insertable modules, also referred to as adaptation units, such as attention projection layers and MLP projection layers. Our goal is to assign an integer rank r u r_{u} to each unit u u under a total rank budget R tot R_{\text{tot}} , yielding a rank allocation vector 𝐫 = ( r 1 , … , r U ) ∈ ℤ U \mathbf{r}=(r_{1},\ldots,r_{U})\in\mathbb{Z}^{U} . The budget controlled in this paper is the total rank budget rather than a strictly matched total number of trainable parameters, so small parameter-count differences may remain when modules have different shapes. Thus, IFCLoRA focuses on how different allocation strategies affect the utilization efficiency of limited adaptation capacity under the same rank budget: ∑ u = 1 U r u = R tot , r u ∈ ℤ , r min ≤ r u ≤ r max . \sum_{u=1}^{U}r_{u}=R_{\text{tot}},\qquad r_{u}\in\mathbb{Z},\qquad r_{\min}\leq r_{u}\leq r_{\max}. (1) In all experiments, we choose feasible budgets satisfying the minimum and maximum rank constraints. Standard LoRA assumes that different layers and modules have similar adaptation requirements and therefore adopts a uniform rank allocation. In contrast, we argue that low-budget performance depends on whether limited capacity is allocated to modules that truly lie on key reasoning paths. The core problem is therefore how to estimate the relative task importance of LoRA-insertable modules before training and use that estimate for one-shot rank allocation. To solve this problem, IFCLoRA first constructs a task-conditioned interaction graph from a small calibration set. It then extracts a topology prior, calibrates it with local task sensitivity, and finally maps the resulting IFC score to a discrete rank allocation under the total budget constraint. 3.2 Task-Conditioned Interaction Graph Construction We represent interactions among LoRA-insertable modules as a task-conditioned sparse directed interaction graph G = ( V , E ) G=(V,E) . Each node v i ∈ V v_{i}\in V corresponds to a LoRA-insertable module, also referred to as an adaptation unit, and each directed edge ( i → j ) ∈ E (i\rightarrow j)\in E indicates that a change in node i i has an observable influence on a later node j j under the current task. The goal is not to recover the full computation circuit exactly, but to build a sparse and tractable structural approximation that carries task-relevant information flow. A node with only the former property may be a passive receiver, while a node with only the latter may not be effectively coupled to the input condition. We therefore combine forward and backward reachability into a topology prior. Target nodes are sorted by depth. The shallowest target node is used as the input-side anchor, and the deepest target node is used as the output-side anchor. We report the measured preprocessing, training-time, and memory overhead in Appendix D . 4 Experiments We evaluate IFCLoRA on mathematical reasoning and general semantic understanding. Section 4.1 describes the setup, Section 4.2 reports the main results, Section 4.3 analyzes rank allocation, and Section 4.4 studies routing components. 4.1 Experimental Setup We evaluate on LLaMA3-8B, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen3-14B (Grattafiori et al. , 2024 ; Yang et al. , 2025 ) . Tasks include GSM8K for mathematical reasoning and SuperGLUE for general semantic understanding (Cobbe et al. , 2021 ; Wang et al. , 2019 ) . GSM8K is evaluated with exact-match accuracy after answer extraction, while SuperGLUE uses official task-specific metrics. The compared methods are LoRA, AdaLoRA, EVA, and IFCLoRA. All methods use the same backbone model, data split, LoRA insertion modules, training protocol, random seeds, and evaluation scripts. LoRA is applied to attention projections ( q , k , v , o q,k,v,o ) and MLP projections (gate, up, down). We mainly study low-rank budgets r = 4 r=4 and r = 8 r=8 , using total rank budget as the main fairness constraint. Unless otherwise stated, each experiment is repeated with three random seeds and reported as mean ± \pm standard deviation. Full training settings, method-specific configurations, reproducibility details, and efficiency measurements are provided in Appendix A . To keep the main table compact, Table 1 reports a compact subset of SuperGLUE subtasks, while the complete nine-subtask breakdown is provided in Appendix B using the same evaluation scripts and metrics. 4.2 Main Experiments Tables 1 and 2 summarize the main experimental results. On GSM8K, IFCLoRA obtains the highest accuracy on all three backbones, reaching 85.44, 82.33, and 65.50 on Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-8B, and LLaMA3-8B, respectively. Compared with LoRA, these results correspond to gains of 0.60, 1.36, and 1.36 percentage points, showing that topology-aware rank allocation can improve mathematical reasoning under limited adaptation capacity. Because all methods are compared under the same total rank budget and IFCLoRA does not change the subsequent LoRA fine-tuning procedure, the gains are attributable to the non-uniform rank-budget allocation rather than additional training capacity. On the SuperGLUE tasks reported in Table 1 , IFCLoRA shows a task-dependent but generally favorable profile. For Qwen3-14B, IFCLoRA achieves the best result on all reported SuperGLUE tasks, with especially clear improvements on BoolQ, CB, and WSC.fixed. For Qwen3-8B, IFCLoRA obtains the highest or tied-highest scores on BoolQ, RTE, and WSC.fixed, while remaining competitive on CB and ReCoRD. For LLaMA3-8B, except for RTE where LoRA is slightly higher, IFCLoRA obtains the best or tied-best result on the remaining reported SuperGLUE tasks. Overall, IFCLoRA provides consistent gains on mathematical reasoning and maintains a task-dependent profile on language-understanding tasks. Compared with adaptive and initialization-based baselines, IFCLoRA shows more consistent performance across the evaluated settings. AdaLoRA does not consistently outperform LoRA under the same low-rank budget, suggesting that training-time dynamic rank adjustment can be sensitive in tight-budget regimes. EVA is competitive on some language-understanding tasks, but its overall performance remains below IFCLoRA. In contrast, IFCLoRA allocates the limited rank budget once before fine-tuning according to the task-conditioned topology prior, leading to more consistent GSM8K performance, with task-dependent behavior on SuperGLUE. (b) Layer-wise average allocated rank across allocation strategies. Figure 4 (a) shows that IFCLoRA learns a clearly non-uniform rank allocation. More capacity is assigned to mid-to-late FFN modules and selected attention projections, while shallow modules are compressed to lower ranks. Similar non-uniform rank profiles have also been observed in recent adaptive-rank LoRA studies, whereas IFCLoRA further links the allocation pattern to task-conditioned information-flow topology (Ed-dib et al. , 2025 ; He et al. , 2025 ; Singh et al. , 2025 ) . This allocation is consistent with prior observations that Transformer FFN layers can act as key-value memories, and suggests that mid-to-late FFN modules may occupy more source-to-sink information-flow paths under the GSM8K calibration distribution (Geva et al. , 2021 ) . In this sense, the learned rank allocation is not merely non-uniform, but aligned with the topology prior used by IFC. The layer-wise view further compares the average allocated rank across strategies. Figure 4 (b) shows that LoRA uses a flat allocation, while AdaLoRA produces a more dispersed dynamic allocation pattern across layers. In contrast, IFCLoRA concentrates rank around a smaller set of layers that are structurally important under the task-conditioned interaction graph. EVA is included as a data-driven initialization and rank-redistribution baseline in the quantitative comparisons in Table 1 and Appendix D ; this subsection focuses on the recorded rank-allocation visualizations for LoRA, AdaLoRA, and IFCLoRA. These observations suggest that low-budget adaptation can benefit from routing capacity toward key modules rather than distributing it uniformly or relying only on diffuse dynamic reallocation. 4.4 Ablation Study Figure 5 : Ablation study and routing-control baselines on Qwen3-8B (GSM8K, r = 4 r=4 ). We ablate the routing score on Qwen3-8B (GSM8K, r = 4 r=4 ), covering routing-control baselines (Random, Depth-biased, and FFN-biased), PageRank, graph-construction ablation (w/o zero ablation), component ablations (w/o Gradient and w/o Topology), and the full IFCLoRA score. As shown in Figure 5 , IFCLoRA achieves the best accuracy (82.33), with w/o Gradient being the strongest ablation (81.88), while w/o zero ablation matches FFN-biased (81.56) and remains below the topology-based variants. The simple routing-control baselines improve over LoRA (80.97) but lag behind w/o Gradient, suggesting that the task-conditioned interaction graph captures allocation signals beyond fixed depth, module type, random assignment, or generic graph centrality. The low w/o Topology result (81.13) further suggests that local gradient-only routing may miss structurally important propagation paths. Overall, these results support the complementarity of global topology, causal zero-ablation tracing, and local task sensitivity. A broader sensitivity analysis over ρ \rho , τ \tau , and calibration size is provided in Appendix C . 5 Discussion Topology-aware rank allocation offers a structural perspective on PEFT. Instead of treating LoRA rank as a uniform hyperparameter or adapting it only from local training-time statistics, IFCLoRA views LoRA-insertable modules as nodes in a task-conditioned interaction graph. This reframes low-budget adaptation as routing limited capacity along task-relevant information-flow paths. The resulting non-uniform rank profiles suggest that useful adaptation capacity is not evenly distributed across Transformer modules, but is shaped by the global organization of task-specific computation. Information-Flow Centrality is the key mechanism that operationalizes this perspective. By combining source-to-sink reachability with local gradient sensitivity, IFC estimates whether a module both receives task-relevant signals and lies on influential propagation paths. This makes the learned rank allocation more interpretable than purely local criteria: the assigned ranks can be traced back to graph structure and task-conditioned perturbation responses. We emphasize, however, that this provides structural evidence for capacity routing rather than a complete causal explanation of the model’s internal mechanism. IFCLoRA has several limitations. The IFC score is a heuristic without formal optimality guarantees: there is no theoretical result establishing that the resulting allocation minimizes downstream task loss under a given budget. The graph construction also assumes a forward-causal node ordering specific to decoder-only Transformers, and whether the approach transfers to encoder-decoder or mixture-of-experts architectures remains an open question. Finally, our experiments cover GSM8K and selected SuperGLUE tasks on three backbones, leaving broader domains and larger scales to be validated. 6 Conclusion and Future Work We presented IFCLoRA, a topology-aware one-shot rank allocation method for LoRA fine-tuning. The method preserves a standard LoRA-like training stage while replacing uniform capacity assignment with a task-conditioned structural prior. Future work includes cheaper graph construction, adaptive recalibration, stronger causal interventions for validating IFC-identified bottlenecks, and extensions to code generation, long-context reasoning, instruction tuning, multimodal adaptation, and broader PEFT design choices such as insertion locations and module types.
